title: Anthropic's BB+ June Credit Rating Issued Without Free Cash Flow Data
summary:
Anthropic generated $16.8 billion in revenue for the third quarter, a 46% increase over the $11.5 billion it posted in the second quarter, as it coordinates up to $95 billion in debt facilities to fund AI hardware. Financial Times documents show that Kroll Bond Rating Agency assigned the company a BB+ credit rating in June, just one notch below investment grade, despite Anthropic not providing EBITDA or free cash flow figures. Kroll had to estimate those missing metrics to arrive at the rating, which preceded a $35 billion Apollo-led chip financing deal.

The expansion relies heavily on support from Broadcom, which guarantees the majority of the Apollo deal and may provide an additional $42 billion in convertible notes for a second $60 billion financing package. Broadcom CEO Hock Tan recently warned that capital access, not chip supply, could become the primary bottleneck for AI growth, likening investors with unrealistic expectations to casino gamblers. Anthropic plans to spend more than $500 billion on computing and infrastructure over the next decade as it seeks to justify its buildout through widespread market adoption.

🚨BREAKING: Anthropic secured a previously undisclosed BB+ credit rating from Kroll Bond Rating Agency in June, just one notch below investment grade, despite not providing free cash flow or EBITDA figures, according to previously unreported documents seen by the FT.

Kroll received revenue, adjusted operating income and internal forecasts, but had to estimate missing metrics and use a separate risk-scoring approach.

The agency also rated $4.4 billion in junior debt directly exposed to Anthropic's credit risk BB+. That debt, part of a $35 billion Apollo-led chip financing, yielded 8.5%, compared with 5.75% for Broadcom-backed senior debt.

Kroll was also not given detailed terms of up to $42 billion in potential convertible notes from Broadcom to finance Anthropic's chip leases.

selectedTweets.text:
Anthropic has a credit rating and it sits just ONE notch below investment grade.

According to the Financial Times, Kroll Bond Rating Agency gave Anthropic a BB+ issuer rating with a stable outlook back in June, and it is only being reported now.

The rating came ahead of the $35 billion Apollo led chip financing that funds more than 1 GW of compute for Anthropic.

$AVGO guarantees most of that deal and only about $4.4 billion of junior debt rides directly on Anthropic's own credit, and it sold at roughly an 8.5% yield versus 5.75% on the senior debt.

Anthropic had ZERO debt on its own balance sheet as of late June. The borrowing sits with partners and special purpose vehicles instead.

This is how the AI buildout is really being paid for and it is why rates and credit markets move AI stocks so much right now.

But what lenders are actually underwriting is REVENUE, and Anthropic just told investors it did $16.8 billion in Q3, up from $11.5 billion in Q2.

As long as that number keeps climbing, the debt behind the compute keeps getting easier to justify.
selectedTweets.quotedTweetText:
Anthropic just reported some absolutely RIDICULOUS numbers!

According to the Financial Times, Anthropic generated $16.8 BILLION in revenue in Q3, up 46% from $11.5 billion in Q2 and that's nearly $5.3 billion in additional quarterly revenue in just THREE months. Anthropic also told investors it was profitable on an adjusted basis AND cash flow positive during the quarter. This is a pretty big deal because one of the biggest concerns surrounding AI companies has been whether they can actually turn this massive demand into a sustainable business, especially when they're spending billions of dollars training models and running inference.

And this is where things get even more interesting. Anthropic is planning to spend MORE THAN $500 BILLION on computing and AI infrastructure over the next decade. Think about that for a second. That's an average of more than $50 billion annually, although the actual spending will likely vary significantly from year to year. All of that money has to go somewhere. We're talking about GPUs, memory, networking equipment, optical components, data centers, power infrastructure, and everything else required to support increasingly powerful AI models. This is exactly why I continue to be so bullish on the broader AI infrastructure trade.

selectedTweets.text:
So spent some more time to look at more DBS conference material: 

- "Two semiconductor giants, $AVGO and $INTC, both stated that breakthroughs in AI will keep demand for chip investment elevated for at least another 2 years. As current supply is insufficient to meet market demand."

- "Current chip production capacity is already far from sufficient to meet demand, and $AVGO CEO expects the shortage to become even more severe in the future." (HKEJ) 

- "Regarding OpenAI, Hock Tan stated that the market had misinterpreted the company because its underlying fundamentals remained strong.

He argued that investors who sell based on a single short-term data point [$50B ARR] are "essentially no different from people gambling in a casino." (eg. Hong Kong Economic Journal):

- Commenting on investors' disappointment in OpenAI’s latest revenue forecast: "by itself, not that bad" on their $50B ARR. (Business Times)

And connected investors' disappointment to a failure to understand the business and excessive expectations like a casino. 

- Tan rejected the proposition that OpenAI was overvalued. It quotes him saying:

"It’s almost like they are in a casino gambling" in regards to investors' unrealistic expectations and lack of understanding on OpenAI.

- Hock Tan if OpenAI and Anthropic achieve widespread market adoption: their attractiveness would substantially strengthen their bargaining power when raising capital. 

But cautioned elevated global interest rates could make capital requirements a constraint for future growth.

- The real driver, he said, is whether frontier AI companies can create models that generate enough value and returns to justify the buildout. (which is fair)

- Most companies are wasting money on tokens. He also warned that most companies just waste money spending tokens like kids in a video arcade.

This part was the most badly worded by Hock Tan given he's running $AVGO. 

But Western media commentary narrowed this down to:
- "Shortage of capital now, AI Investors are gamblers". 

In the conference, Broadcom's CEO was actually defending frontier lab valuations and giving cautiously bullish statements about AI infrastructure demand. 

While citing rising interest rates as a potential constraint that larger revenue or adoption could overcome. 

Cherry picking quotes out of context disorts the actual messaging. 

TLDR:

- Large and elevated AI semi demand, semi supply insufficient to meet market demand. At least another 2 years of elevated spend

- OpenAI valuations defensible, people who sell based on extreme expectations for the company are like casino gamblers. 

- Tan stated markets had misinterpreted OpenAI's ARR because its underlying fundamentals remained strong.

-  Frontier labs if they achieve widespread adoption / revenue would strengthen capital raising, which overpower headwinds from raising interest rates. 

Lot of $AVGO CEO remarks looks heavily nuanced, which Western media coverage distored.

selectedTweets.bestBit: Broadcom is backing about $42 billion more in a newer $60 billion chip package for Anthropic too
selectedTweets.text:
🦔Anthropic got a credit rating back in June that only came out this week. Kroll Bond Rating Agency gave it a BB+, the best junk rating you can get and one step below investment grade. The FT says it landed just before Apollo and Blackstone lined up $35 billion to buy chips for Anthropic.

My Take
Kroll didn’t get to see much. Anthropic gave it revenue, run-rate revenue, adjusted operating income and its own forecast, but no free cash flow, so the analysts guessed at that part. I think the grade is generous. Oracle sits one notch higher at BBB- and everyone treats it as a company in trouble. My guess is Moody’s and S&P come in lower once the S-1 shows full results, since adjusted numbers tend to leave out the expensive stuff.

Most of that $35 billion got borrowed at about 5.75%, a low rate for a junk-rated company, because Broadcom agreed to cover lenders if the chips ever have to be sold at a loss. Broadcom is backing about $42 billion more in a newer $60 billion chip package for Anthropic too. Lenders seem fine with that, and so does Apollo, which put part of the first deal into its own annuity company, Athene. I’m less comfortable with it. If Anthropic ever falls behind on those leases, Broadcom ends up holding a mountain of used chips, and I don’t think Broadcom’s stock reflects that risk today.

Hedgie🤗
